planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Buttercup is a classic clear-yellow crocosmia, a color less common than the reds and oranges typical of the genus.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Buttercup bears arching, one-sided sprays of clear, bright yellow, tubular flowers above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a cheerful, sunny color that stands apart from the more common red and orange crocosmia cultivars. Its flowers draw hummingbirds and make good cut flowers, holding well in a vase. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection, and give it consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best flowering display.

common_name: Citronella Crocosmia (Lemon-Yellow with Dark Eye Montbretia)

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Citronella bears lemon-yellow flowers marked with a small dark central eye, a distinctive pattern within the genus.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Citronella bears arching, one-sided sprays of clear lemon-yellow, tubular flowers, each marked with a small contrasting dark eye at the throat, above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer, a subtly patterned twist on the classic yellow crocosmia color. Hummingbirds visit the flowers reliably, and cut stems hold up well in arrangements. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection, and provide consistently moist, well-drained soil for the best display.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Babylon is one of the largest-flowered crocosmia cultivars available, with individual blooms notably bigger than most named selections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Babylon produces some of the largest individual flowers in the genus, bearing arching sprays of bold orange-red, trumpet-shaped blooms considerably bigger than most named crocosmia cultivars, held above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. Its outsized flowers make a strong architectural statement in the border and are a favorite of hummingbirds, as well as an excellent long-lasting cut flower. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection.

planting.note: Divide corm chains in early spring before growth resumes, or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Hellfire bears deep, saturated blood-red flowers, among the darkest reds available in the genus.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Hellfire produces arching, one-sided sprays of deep, saturated blood-red, tubular flowers, among the darkest, most intense reds available among named crocosmia cultivars, held above bold, pleated, sword-like foliage in mid to late summer. Its dramatic color makes it a strong companion to the more famous Lucifer within a hot-colored border, and hummingbirds visit the flowers reliably through the bloom season. Divide congested corm clumps every three to four years in early spring, since crowded corms produce progressively fewer and shorter flower spikes over time. In colder parts of its range, mulch heavily over the corms for winter protection.

common_name: Tinkerbell Agapanthus (Dwarf Variegated Pale Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Tinkerbell is a dwarf, variegated agapanthus well suited to container growing and small border spaces.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, in a container or garden bed. Tinkerbell forms a compact, dwarf clump of narrow, strappy leaves edged in a crisp cream-white variegation, giving the plant ornamental value even before bloom, topped in summer by rounded clusters of pale, soft blue, trumpet-shaped flowers on short scapes held just above the foliage. Its small scale and attractive variegated foliage make it especially well suited to containers, small borders, and edging where larger agapanthus cultivars would be out of proportion. In regions colder than its hardiness range, grow it in a container and bring it into a cool, frost-free space for winter, or apply heavy mulch over the crown if planted in the ground near the edge of its hardiness zone. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.
